column1: What is the normal physiological range of pH in human arterial blood?
column2: The normal range is $7.35$ to $7.45$.

column1: An arterial blood pH value below $7.35$ indicates _____, whereas a pH value above $7.45$ indicates _____.
column2: acidosis; alkalosis

column1: How are extracellular hydrogen ion concentration $[H^+]$ and blood pH mathematically related?
column2: They are inversely related; as $[H^+]$ increases, pH decreases.

column1: What ion exchange occurs across cell membranes to maintain electroneutrality during extracellular acidosis?
column2: $H^+$ shifts into the cells in exchange for $K^+$ moving out into the extracellular fluid.

column1: What electrolyte complication typically arises when cells buffer excess extracellular hydrogen ions ($H^+$)?
column2: Hyperkalemia, because $K^+$ exits cells to balance the intracellular movement of $H^+$.

column1: What is the primary source of daily acid production in the human body under normal conditions?
column2: Cellular metabolism, which produces $\text{CO}_2$ that hydrates into carbonic acid ($\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$).

column1: Approximately how much total hydrogen ion load ($H^+$) is produced daily by cellular metabolism via $\text{CO}_2$ formation?
column2: Greater than $12,500\text{ mEq/day}$.

column1: Which organ is primarily responsible for excreting the volatile acid load generated as $\text{CO}_2$?
column2: The lungs.

column1: What are the three main chemical buffer systems present in blood?
column2: Proteins, hemoglobin, and the carbonic acid-bicarbonate system.

column1: Why are plasma proteins effective as chemical buffers in blood?
column2: Because both their free carboxyl ($-\text{COOH}$) and free amino ($-\text{NH}_2$) groups can dissociate.

column1: How does deoxyhemoglobin act as a buffer in systemic tissue capillaries?
column2: Deoxyhemoglobin binds free protons ($H^+$) generated from carbonic acid dissociation and transports them toward the lungs.

column1: What occurs in pulmonary capillaries when oxygen binds to hemoglobin regarding proton buffering?
column2: Oxygen uptake releases bound $H^+$ from hemoglobin, allowing $H^+$ to combine with $\text{HCO}_3^-$ to form $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$.

column1: Which enzyme catalyzes the conversion of $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ into $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in pulmonary circulation for exhalation?
column2: Carbonic anhydrase.

column1: What is the normal standard value for arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide ($P_{\text{aCO}_2}$)?
column2: Approximately $40\text{ mm Hg}$.

column1: How does the respiratory center respond when arterial $P_{\text{CO}_2}$ rises due to increased tissue metabolism?
column2: Ventilation is stimulated, increasing the rate of pulmonary excretion of $\text{CO}_2$ to return $P_{\text{CO}_2}$ toward normal.

column1: What primary apical membrane exchanger is responsible for renal $H^+$ secretion in the proximal tubule?
column2: The $\text{Na}^+$-$H^+$ exchanger 3 (NHE3).

column1: What provides the driving force for secondary active transport via the apical NHE3 exchanger in proximal tubule cells?
column2: The low intracellular $\text{Na}^+$ concentration maintained by basolateral $\text{Na}^+$-$\text{K}^+$ ATPase.

column1: In the proximal tubule, secreted $H^+$ combines with filtered $\text{HCO}_3^-$ to form which compound in the lumen?
column2: Carbonic acid ($\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$).

column1: What action does apical carbonic anhydrase perform on luminal $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ in the proximal tubule?
column2: It catalyzes the breakdown of luminal $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ into $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{CO}_2$.

column1: What percentage of the filtered load of bicarbonate ($\text{HCO}_3^-$) is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?
column2: Approximately $80\%$.

column1: Formula: Serum Anion Gap (AG)
column2: $\text{AG} = [\text{Na}^+] - ([\text{Cl}^-] + [\text{HCO}_3^-])$

column1: What is the normal reference range for the serum Anion Gap (AG)?
column2: Approximately $10\text{ to }14\text{ mEq/L}$ (average $12\text{ mEq/L}$).

column1: What unmeasured anions (UA) normally compose the serum Anion Gap?
column2: Plasma proteins (in anionic form), phosphate ($\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$), sulfate ($\text{SO}_4^{2-}$), and organic acids.

column1: An Anion Gap greater than _____ indicates High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis.
column2: $16\text{ mEq/L}$

column1: How does severe hypoalbuminemia (decreased plasma albumin) affect the measured serum Anion Gap?
column2: It decreases the serum Anion Gap because albumin is a major unmeasured anion.

column1: How does an accumulation of organic anions like lactate or ketoacids affect the serum Anion Gap?
column2: It increases the serum Anion Gap.

column1: What are the five common parameters measured in a standard Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) analysis?
column2: $\text{pH}$, $P_{\text{aCO}_2}$, Anion Gap (AG), Base Excess (BE), and $[\text{HCO}_3^-]$.

column1: How does a decrease in plasma concentration of cations like $Ca^{2+}$ or $Mg^{2+}$ impact the serum Anion Gap?
column2: It increases the calculated Anion Gap by reducing total unmeasured cations.

column1: Concept: High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis
column2: Definition: A form of metabolic acidosis caused by an accumulation of fixed organic acids (such as lactate or ketoacids) that increase unmeasured anions.

column1: Process: Proximal tubule bicarbonate reabsorption (luminal phase)
column2: Secreted $H^+$ combines with filtered $\text{HCO}_3^-$ to form $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$, which apical carbonic anhydrase degrades to $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ for cellular entry.

column1: Process: Proximal tubule bicarbonate reabsorption (intracellular phase)
column2: Intracellular $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ are converted by carbonic anhydrase into $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$, which dissociates into $H^+$ (secreted) and $\text{HCO}_3^-$ (reabsorbed into blood).

column1: Why does acute accumulation of lactic acid lead to an elevated serum Anion Gap?
column2: Lactic acid dissociates into $H^+$ (which consumes $\text{HCO}_3^-$) and lactate, an unmeasured anion that replaces bicarbonate.

column1: What is the physiological role of renal tubular hydrogen ion secretion?
column2: It allows the nephron to reabsorb filtered bicarbonate and excrete excess non-volatile metabolic acid.

column1: When arterial $P_{\text{CO}_2}$ rises by $15\text{ mm Hg}$ due to inhaled $\text{CO}_2$, why does alveolar $P_{\text{CO}_2}$ rise by only a fraction of that amount?
column2: Because hyperventilation is triggered, accelerating pulmonary $\text{CO}_2$ elimination.

column1: The principal mechanism of non-volatile acid excretion in the kidneys involves hydrogen ion ($H^+$) secretion in which nephron segments?
column2: The proximal tubule, distal tubule, and collecting duct.

column1: Cloze: In blood gas analysis, a pH strictly above _____ represents alkalosis.
Cloze: In blood gas analysis, a pH strictly below _____ represents acidosis.
Which form of hemoglobin acts as a stronger buffer for protons ($H^+$): oxyhemoglobin or deoxyhemoglobin?
column2: Deoxyhemoglobin.

column1: How does the hydration of metabolic $\text{CO}_2$ in tissue capillary blood affect local pH if unbuffered?
column2: It forms carbonic acid, which dissociates into $H^+$ and lowers local pH.

column1: What happens to extracellular electroneutrality if $H^+$ ions enter cells without potassium exchange?
column2: Intracellular space becomes abnormally positively charged; $K^+$ outflow prevents this charge imbalance.

column1: In the formula $\text{AG} = \text{UA} - \text{UC}$, what do the acronyms UA and UC represent?
column2: Unmeasured Anions (UA) and Unmeasured Cations (UC).

column1: If a patient's lab values are $[\text{Na}^+] = 140\text{ mEq/L}$, $[\text{Cl}^-] = 104\text{ mEq/L}$, and $[\text{HCO}_3^-] = 24\text{ mEq/L}$, what is their calculated Anion Gap?
Why is the carbonic acid-bicarbonate system considered the primary extracellular buffer in blood?
column2: Because its components are highly regulated by both the respiratory system ($\text{CO}_2$) and renal system ($\text{HCO}_3^-$).

column1: What term describes the laboratory measurement indicating the difference between buffer base present and normal buffer base level?
column2: Base Excess (BE).

column1: Under resting conditions, where is the vast majority ($80\%$) of filtered bicarbonate reabsorbed in the kidney?
column2: In the proximal convoluted tubule.

column1: What is the effect of increased plasma protein concentration on the calculated serum Anion Gap?
column2: It increases the serum Anion Gap because plasma proteins carry net negative charges (unmeasured anions).

column1: What primary transporter on the basolateral membrane of renal proximal tubule cells maintains low intracellular $\text{Na}^+$?
column2: The $\text{Na}^+$-$\text{K}^+$ ATPase.

column1: In addition to reabsorbing filtered bicarbonate, how do the kidneys contribute to acid-base recovery during chronic acidosis?
column2: They generate new bicarbonate ions and excrete $H^+$ tied to titratable acids and ammonium.

column1: How does hyperventilation affect arterial $P_{\text{aCO}_2}$ and blood pH?
column2: It lowers $P_{\text{aCO}_2}$ and elevates blood pH.

column1: Why does arterial pH technically reflect acidosis whenever it falls below $7.40$, even if within the normal clinical buffer range?
column2: Because $7.40$ is the physiological midpoint norm for arterial plasma pH.

column1: What is the net effect of cellular buffering during systemic acid overload on blood electrolyte levels?
column2: Extracellular $H^+$ is reduced while extracellular $K^+$ increases (hyperkalemia).

column1: What component of red blood cells allows rapid conversion between $\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$?
column2: Intracellular carbonic anhydrase.

column1: If a patient has a serum $[\text{Na}^+] = 137$, $[\text{Cl}^-] = 90$, and $[\text{HCO}_3^-] = 22\text{ mEq/L}$, what is their calculated Anion Gap?
What classification of acid-base disorder is indicated by a calculated Anion Gap of $25\text{ mEq/L}$?
column2: High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis.

column1: Which chemical group on plasma proteins acts as a base by accepting protons during acidosis?
column2: The free amino group ($-\text{NH}_2$, forming $-\text{NH}_3^+$).

column1: Which chemical group on plasma proteins acts as an acid by donating protons during alkalosis?
column2: The free carboxyl group ($-\text{COOH}$, forming $-\text{COO}^-$).
